topics: 📏 Two Cubits in Shushan HaBirah — a built-in safeguard against misusing Temple funds
🥚 One Testicle or Two? — Rabbi Yishmael's visual test vs. Rabbi Akiva's physical test, and a real dispute it caused
🦵 Extra Legs, Donkey Hooves, and Uneven Thighs — the mishna's catalogue of limb blemishes
🐷 Ila's Additions — a round human-like eye, a pig-like mouth, and a damaged tongue
👂 Doubled Ears and Counting Tail Joints — Rav Huna's ruling overturned by a baraita

overview.title: 📖 Overview: Cataloguing Limbs, Jaws, and a Contested Testicle
overview.subtitle: Bekhorot 40a–40b
overview.hebrewSource: בַּעַל חָמֵשׁ רַגְלַיִם, אוֹ שֶׁאֵין לוֹ אֶלָּא שָׁלֹשׁ, וְשֶׁרַגְלָיו קְלוּטוֹת כְּשֶׁל חֲמוֹר, וְהַשָּׁחוּל וְהַכָּסוּל
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: After a brief note on the Temple's two measuring cubits (used to prevent misuse of consecrated funds), the daf turns to a mishna disputing how to determine whether a firstborn has one testicle or two — a disagreement vivid enough to spark a real halakhic clash between Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Yohanan ben Nuri over an actual case. Further mishnayot catalogue blemishes of the legs and hooves (extra or missing legs, donkey-like hooves, uneven thighs), then record the blemishes counted by the expert Ila, including some the Sages initially hadn't heard of but ultimately accepted. The daf closes with disputes over doubled ears and how many tail joints a kid or lamb needs to avoid being blemished.

slides.title: 📏 Two Cubits, One Safeguard
slides.hebrewSource: אוּמָּנִין נוֹטְלִין בַּקְּטַנָּה, וּמַחְזִירִין בַּגְּדוֹלָה, שֶׁלֹּא יָבוֹאוּ לִידֵי מְעִילָה
slides.label: Why the Temple kept two measuring cubits:
slides.text: One cubit in the chamber of Shushan HaBirah was a half-fingerbreadth longer than Moses' cubit, the other a full fingerbreadth longer. Artisans were paid using the smaller measure but had to return equivalent work measured by the larger one — a built-in margin ensuring they never inadvertently took more from the Temple treasury than they earned, avoiding the sin of misusing consecrated property (מְעִילָה). This same 'fingerbreadth' unit, one-quarter of a handbreadth, is used elsewhere to measure the flesh gap between a firstborn's tail vertebrae.

slides.title: 🥚 How Do You Know If It Has One Testicle or Two?
slides.subtitle: A dispute vivid enough to become a real, contested case

lines.speaker: Mishna
lines.text: A firstborn with no testicles, or only one, may be slaughtered — but how do you determine the count without cutting the animal open?

lines.speaker: R' Yishmael
lines.text: Simple: two scrotal sacs means two testicles; one sac means only one testicle.

lines.speaker: R' Akiva
lines.text: Not so fast — seat the animal on its rump and press the sac. If a testicle is there, it will eventually emerge.

lines.speaker: Real case
lines.text: In Piran of Beit Menaḥem: pressed, nothing emerged — animal slaughtered — the testicle was found stuck to the loins all along! R' Akiva permitted the meat; R' Yoḥanan ben Nuri forbade it.

lines.speaker: R' Akiva
lines.text: 'Until when will you consume the property of the Jewish people?!' (by needlessly forbidding valid meat)

lines.speaker: R' Yoḥanan b. Nuri
lines.text: 'Until when will you feed the Jewish people sacrificial meat outside the Temple?!' (since the testicle was there all along — no blemish existed)

callout.label: The stakes:
callout.text: A single ambiguous pressing test led two great Sages to accuse each other of causing either needless loss or forbidden consumption.

slides.title: 🦵 New Mishna: Leg and Hoof Blemishes
slides.subtitle: Extra limbs, wrong hooves, and uneven thighs all permit slaughter
rows: Five legs, or only three
Extra or missing limb
Rav Huna: applies fully to forelegs; a missing/extra HIND leg makes it a tereifa too
Hooves closed like a donkey's (קָלוּט)
Round, undivided hooves
Rav Pappa: counts even if partly split, as long as rounded
Shaḥul (שָׁחוּל)
Thighbone dislocated
Kasul (כָּסוּל)
One thigh higher/displaced relative to the other
Saru'a (שָׂרוּעַ)
One thigh longer than the other
A Torah term (Leviticus 22:23) for disqualification from the altar

callout.label: Broken bones count too:
callout.text: A broken foreleg or hind leg bone is a blemish even if not visibly conspicuous, so long as it's noticeable from how the animal walks (Rav Pappa).

slides.title: 🐷 Ila's Three Additions
slides.subtitle: The Sages initially hesitated, then accepted all three

boxes.title: Round Eye
items: An eye round like a human's (not an animal's usual shape)
Gemara connects it to a parallel dispute in Nidda over identifying a miscarried fetus

boxes.title: Pig-Like Mouth
items: Upper lip overlapping the lower, pig-fashion
Rav Pappa: counts even without a pointed snout, as long as it overlaps

boxes.title: Damaged Tongue
items: Most of the 'speaking segment' of the tongue removed (Rabbi Yehuda's definition)
Distinguished from removing most of the tongue generally

callout.label: Related ruling:
callout.text: A lower jaw protruding beyond the upper is also a blemish for an animal specifically when the jaw contains bone — unlike a person, where any lip overlap counts, since 'a man of the seed of Aaron' requires an ordinary human appearance.

slides.title: 👂 Doubled Ears and a Refuted Ruling on Tail Joints
slides.subtitle: Rav Huna's measurements are overturned by a baraita
rows: Doubled ear with its own cartilage
A blemish
Doubled ear without its own cartilage (just extra skin)
Not a blemish
Kid's tail with only 1 joint (correct baraita)
A blemish — Rav Huna's claim of '2 joints' is refuted
Lamb's tail with only 2 joints (correct baraita)
A blemish — Rav Huna's claim of '3 joints' is refuted
Rabbi Ḥanina ben Antigonus's list
Also includes: a wart in the eye, a dislocated jaw-bone, and eyes/ears mismatched in size 'by sight, not just by measurement'

callout.label: Rav Huna's mistake:
callout.text: He assumed both clauses of the baraita referred to a kid; in fact the second clause switches to discussing a lamb — explaining why his numbers were off.

summary.principle: The mishnayot build an increasingly detailed catalogue of physical blemishes — limbs, hooves, jaw, eyes, ears, and tail — each defined with enough precision to prevent both needless financial loss and improper consumption of consecrated meat.

flowSteps.content: 📏 The Temple's two measuring cubits protect against misuse of consecrated funds
🥚 R' Yishmael's visual test vs. R' Akiva's physical test for counting testicles — a real case divides the Sages
🦵 Extra/missing legs, donkey hooves, and uneven thighs all permit slaughter

columns.content: 🐷 Ila's added blemishes (round eye, pig mouth, damaged tongue) are accepted
👂 Doubled ears and tail-joint counts are precisely defined, correcting Rav Huna's error

flowSteps.content: 🎓 Key Principle: precise, agreed-upon definitions for every blemish protect against both wasting Jewish property and eating forbidden sacrificial meat

quiz.q: Why did the Temple use two different measuring cubits, one slightly longer than the other?
o: To confuse foreign visitors
So artisans would be paid using the smaller measure but return equivalent work measured by the larger one, preventing misuse of consecrated funds
One was for gold and one for silver only, with no other purpose
There is no reason given
quiz.e: The two cubits created a safety margin so that artisans working with Temple property would never inadvertently take more value than they gave, avoiding me'ila (misuse of consecrated property).

quiz.q: In the incident at Piran of Beit Menaḥem, what caused the dispute between Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Yoḥanan ben Nuri?
o: Whether the animal was a firstborn at all
A pressing test found no testicle, but after slaughter a testicle was found stuck to the loins; Rabbi Akiva permitted the meat while Rabbi Yoḥanan ben Nuri forbade it
The animal had five legs
They disputed the animal's age
quiz.e: Since the testicle never emerged during Rabbi Akiva's test but was found attached to the loins after slaughter, the two sages disagreed about whether this constituted a valid blemish, leading to a sharp exchange.

quiz.q: According to Rav Huna, what is the difference between a missing/extra foreleg and a missing/extra hind leg on a firstborn?
o: There is no difference
A missing/extra hind leg makes the animal a tereifa in addition to being blemished, unlike a foreleg
Only forelegs count as blemishes at all
Hind legs are never considered a blemish
quiz.e: Rav Huna rules that an issue with a hind leg is more severe, rendering the animal a tereifa as well as blemished, since a removed hind leg is a classic tereifa condition.

quiz.q: What is the practical difference the Gemara identifies between a lower jaw protruding on a person versus on an animal?
o: There is no difference between the two cases
For an animal it is a blemish only if the protruding jaw contains bone, while for a person any lip protrusion counts, based on the requirement that a priest have an ordinary human appearance
Jaw protrusion is never a blemish for either
Only priests can have this blemish
quiz.e: Rav Pappa resolves the apparent contradiction: an animal's protruding jaw is a blemish only when bone is involved, whereas for a human priest ('a man of the seed of Aaron'), any lip protrusion disqualifies him from an ordinary appearance.

quiz.q: How does the Gemara explain Rav Huna's mistaken ruling about the number of tail joints required for a kid versus a lamb?
o: Rav Huna never made an error
He mistakenly assumed both clauses of a baraita referred to a kid, when the second clause actually switched to discussing a lamb
The baraita was itself corrupted beyond understanding
He confused tail joints with ear cartilage
quiz.e: The Gemara explains that Rav Huna was misled by the mishna's structure, thinking both parts discussed the kid, when a baraita clarifies that the second part actually refers to a lamb.
